S1.text: "I fear not the man who has practised 10,000 kicks once, but the man who has practised one kick 10,000 times." Attributed to Bruce Lee. Fighters, poets and emperors over 2,600 years kept saying the same thing, so swipe and see.

"The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing." Archilochus, Greek poet, about 2,600 years ago. The fox is clever, but the hedgehog wins, because it does its one thing every single time.
"To be everywhere is to be nowhere." Seneca wrote this to a friend who kept jumping from book to book. He added that a plant moved too often never grows strong.
锲而不舍，金石可镂 "Keep carving and never stop, and even metal and stone will give way." Xunzi also wrote the other half: carve and then stop, and even rotten wood won't break.

"We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit." Will Durant wrote this in 1926, summing up Aristotle. Greatness isn't one big day, it's one small thing done again and again.
"Concentration is the secret of strength." Ralph Waldo Emerson said it holds in politics, in war and in trade. The same goes for the body.
"Put all your eggs in the one basket, and watch that basket." Mark Twain flipped the old advice in 1894. Don't spread yourself thin, choose one basket and guard it.
"Concentrate every minute on doing what's in front of you." Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire and still wrote this note to himself. If an emperor could do one thing at a time, so can we.

Hokusai drew from the age of 6, and in 1834 he wrote that nothing he made before 70 was worth much. Only at 73 did he feel he was starting to understand how birds, fish and trees grow. One craft, a whole lifetime.

Patanjali, Yoga Sutra 1.14: practice holds firm when it's done for a long time, without a break, with devotion. That's what Ashtanga asks of you: same asana, same order, every morning. Try one Mysore morning at aybkk.net.

S2.text: In 1991, at a dinner, Bill Gates and Warren Buffett were asked for the one thing behind their success. Both wrote down the same word. You'll find it on the last slide.
In 1519, Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico and sank his own ships. With no way back, his men had one direction left. When there's no plan B, plan A gets everything you've got.
"If he sends reinforcements everywhere, he will everywhere be weak." Sun Tzu wrote this about armies about 2,500 years ago. Spread your strength over ten fronts, and you're weak on all ten.

On December 17, 1903, the Wright brothers' first flight lasted 12 seconds. Two bicycle makers had spent years on one problem: how to control a plane in the air. Twelve seconds changed how the whole world travels.
In 1501, Michelangelo took on a block of marble that other sculptors had given up on. He worked on it for 3 years. It became David.
In 1997, Apple was close to going under. Steve Jobs came back and cut the product line down to four. Saying no to dozens of products saved the company.

Jiro Ono has spent more than 70 years making one thing: sushi. His tiny 10-seat restaurant in a Tokyo subway station won three Michelin stars. There's no menu of a hundred dishes, just one thing done better every year.

On October 12, 2019, in Vienna, Eliud Kipchoge ran a marathon in 1:59:40, the first person ever under two hours (unofficial). He had missed by 25 seconds in 2017. He then spent two more years on one goal.

In 1927, a 12-year-old boy named Pattabhi Jois watched Krishnamacharya teach in Hassan, a town near Mysore. He started the next day, and kept practising the same method for the rest of his life. Ashtanga reached the world through him.
The word Gates and Buffett both wrote was "focus." In Ashtanga, focus looks like this: same asana, same order, every morning. Try one Mysore morning at aybkk.net.
